text.p: The following are the main stories from Thursday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Organs can be transplanted after brain death, according to new law passed in Bundestag lower house of parliament
- Leader of the liberal Free Democrats (FDP) Wolfgang Gerhard accuses the Christian Social Union (CSU) of anti-euro populism. European MPs also criticise Stoiber over his euro remarks
- Bonn does not want to name any candidates for NATO expansion
- Row in the finance planning council of the federal and regional state authorities. Finance Minister Theo Waigel is headed for confrontation.
- The German government will transfer 25 percent of its total capital in Deutsche Telekom to the state development agency Kreditanstalt fuer Wiederaufbau (KfW) in two steps in 1997 and 1998.
HANDELSBLATT
- IG Metall threatens to go on strike for innovative early retirement schemes.
- Bundestag lower house of parliament passes law on organ transplantation
- Finance Minister Theo Waigel sees room for play for credits.
- New record high on DAX share index
- Chief Economist of Merill Lynch says investors should not make a decision that would not also be sensible after the launch of Europe's planned single currency, the euro
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- German lower house of parliament passes law on organ transplantation
- Finance Minister Theo Waigel says state spending must be cut
- Volkswagen is first company to introduce innovative early retirement scheme
- Cost of living in former East Germany have risen in last six months
- Ifo research agency says business climate has improved
DIE WELT
- Lower house of parliament passes organ transplantation law
- Finance Minister Theo Waigel says opposition Social Democrats' (SPD) attack his budget. SPD parliamentary group leader Rudolf Scharping says 1996 budget was unconstitutional.
- Bonn ruling coalition want to pass tax reform in Bundestag lower house today.
- Upturn in jobs market is possible, Ifo institute says

- Talks for innovative early retirement schemes break down. IG Metall trade union threatens battle for jobs. But head of German employers federation Dieter Hundt says VW model for such schemes would not apply to metal sector.
